hints: Focus on what keeps molecules close together as a liquid, which is forces between molecules, not bonds inside a molecule.
Recall the two conditions for hydrogen bonding: H bonded to N, O or F, plus a lone pair on N, O or F of a neighbour. Check which molecule meets both.
Connect the much stronger intermolecular attraction in one substance to a much higher boiling point, so it stays liquid at room temperature while the other is already a gas.
walkthrough:
**Separate Inside From Between**

Think like a teacher with you. Boiling and state depend on breaking forces *between* molecules, not covalent bonds or ionisation *inside* atoms.

So we can ignore properties of single O or S atoms and look for: what intermolecular force is present in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ but missing in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$?

**Spot Hydrogen Bonding in Water**

Water meets both rules for hydrogen bonding. H is directly bonded to very electronegative O, and O has two lone pairs to accept.

$$\text{O}^{\delta-}-\text{H}^{\delta+} \cdots :\text{O}(\text{H}_2)$$ 
This $\text{H}^{\delta+} \cdots$ lone pair attraction is much stronger than ordinary dipole-dipole forces, so lots of energy is needed to separate $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules.

**Compare With H2S and Conclude**

In $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, S is larger and much less electronegative than O. The H-S bond is barely polar and S cannot form effective hydrogen bonds.

$\text{H}_2\text{S}$ has only weaker permanent dipole-dipole and London forces, so it boils very easily and is a gas at room temperature and pressure, while strongly hydrogen-bonded $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is a liquid.

options.A: Ionisation energy tells us how hard it is to remove an electron from a gaseous atom. It does not control attraction between neutral molecules, so it cannot explain boiling point or physical state.
options.B: The O-H covalent bond is indeed stronger than S-H, but boiling does not break covalent bonds. It only overcomes intermolecular forces, so this is a classic inside versus between confusion.
options.C: Correct and reassuring. Significant hydrogen bonding exists between $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules due to highly electronegative O with lone pairs, but not between $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ molecules. This gives water much stronger intermolecular attraction and a much higher boiling point, so it is liquid while $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ is gas.
options.D: This reverses the London force trend. Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London) forces increase with more electrons and larger electron cloud. $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ has more electrons than $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so its London forces are actually stronger, yet it is still a gas because it lacks hydrogen bonding.
